newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea prosecutors demand death for Chun Doo Hwan.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea prosecutors demand death for Chun Doo Hwan.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors on Thursday demanded an appeals court uphold a death sentence on former president Chun Doo Hwan for staging a 1979 coup and ordering a massacre to quell resistance.
Prosecutors also called on the court to extend to life in prison a 22-1/2 year jail sentence imposed on ex-president Roh Tae-woo in August.
Earlier, an angry judge dismissed as a witness a third former president, Choi Kyu-hah, an ailing recluse who refused to answer prosecution questions after being forced to attend the court.
Choi, 77, was caretaker head of state for 10 turbulent months between the assassination of presidential strongman Park Chung-hee in October 1979 and Chun's grab for power.
He holds many of the secrets of the dramatic events surrounding the putsch but has stubbornly ignored demands to appear in court to testify.

Chun was convicted of leading the coup, ordering a massacre of pro-democracy demonstrators in May 1980 in the southern city of Kwangju and amassing a slush fund worth hundreds of millions of dollars from corporate pay-offs.
Roh was sentenced on similar charges of mutiny, treason and bribery. Both are appealing the verdicts.

Prosecutors also demanded jail sentences of 10 years to life for 14 former aides to Roh and Chun appearing in the same appeals court. One was acquitted in the criminal trial and the others sentenced to between four and 10 years.
The appeal on charges of mutiny and treason is now over. A separate appeal on the corruption convictions continues.
Chun and Roh left the courtroom minutes before Choi entered after defence lawyers launched a bitter protest against forcing three former heads of state to stand together in court.
"It is a tragedy in our constitutional history that three former presidents are appearing in the same court," one defence lawyer said before the judge allowed the two to step out.
Prosecutors say Chun forced Choi from office, but Chun maintains Choi asked him to step in to save the country from unrest.
Choi refused to take an oath after he entered the high court, hobbling on a cane.

"It is regretful that I am standing in this court against my will," he said in a prepared statement. "Such a precedent, a former president appearing in court, could damage our national interests and hurt our image abroad. It can also create a political controversy."
Later he complained of back pains. "I am sick. I cannot stand or sit up for long," he said.
After the judge dismissed his complaint and ordered the prosecution to continue questioning, Choi said: "You may ask questions but I am not going to answer."
Angered by his stonewalling, the judge halted proceedings, saying it was meaningless to continue. "By law the witness deserves punishment, but it is not worth punishing you. You may go," he said.
Choi bowed as he limped from the court supported by aides, having stayed only 40 minutes.
The opposition National Congress for New Politics angrily accused Choi of hypocrisy, saying in a statement he was simply protecting his "egotistic and illusive interest".
The Citizens Coalition for Economic Justice, a leading civic group, said in a statement: "Choi will not be able to escape the historical judgment of dismissing the public's request to testify.
